articles.title: Fox News predicts Democrats will win House in midterms for first time this cycle
articles.summary: Fox News has predicted Democrats will win the House in the November midterm elections, the outlet’s first time predicting a Democratic win of either chamber during this election cycle. “Combined with Democrats’ candidate quality improvements and a Republican-led redistricting effort that could fall short of expectations, the House is likely out of reach for the…
articles.body:
Fox News has predicted Democrats will win the House in the November midterm elections, the outlet’s first time predicting a Democratic win of either chamber during this election cycle.

“Combined with Democrats’ candidate quality improvements and a Republican-led redistricting effort that could fall short of expectations, the House is likely out of reach for the GOP this year,” Fox News contributor Rémy Numa wrote about his latest power rankings , which were released Tuesday.

The rankings showed Democrats winning 219 House seats to lock in a majority, with 20 races shifted toward Democrats. Republicans are expected to keep 198 seats, with 18 other races considered toss-ups.

“On a good night for the Democrats, the party will hold around 237 seats, or a gain of 22 from their current position,” Numa wrote. “That’s because toss-up seats have mostly fallen in one party’s direction in previous elections.”

He later added that a “great night” for Democrats would be to win some of the seats that lean Republican, giving them a boost with 249 seats. But if the toss-up seats go for Republicans, the GOP could end up with 216 seats, short of a majority but leaving the Democrats “with a mere two-vote cushion in the House.”

Numa said GOP losses and potential Democratic gains would be the result of rising gas, diesel and grocery prices, writing that voters “keep saying they are feeling the pressure of those increases and blame Republicans for them.”

The rankings show both parties are favored to win 47 seats in the Senate, with Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas named as toss-ups, any of which can determine who takes control of the upper chamber. Winning those seats gives Democrats the majority “with two seats to spare,” Numa wrote, adding that the forecast still sees a path to victory for the GOP.

The toss-ups have been locked in through the summer, but he added that some states leaning Republican could be close. Numa said Republican Senate candidate Michele Tafoya has made gains in Minnesota, but she is narrowly behind Democratic opponent Peggy Flanagan. He projects Flanagan ahead of Tafoya at 47-43, with the state shifting from likely Democrat to lean Democrat.

“Republicans are fully united behind Tafoya, while 9 in 10 Democrats say they’ll support Flanagan’s bid. Independents are much less settled: 38 percent back Tafoya, 32 percent support Flanagan and 29 percent haven’t decided,” he wrote.

Polling weeks away from the midterms has shown Democrats winning the majority in the House amid the president’s sinking popularity and rising concerns over the cost of living and energy prices. Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) gives Democrats a 77 percent probability of winning the House as of Wednesday, likely holding 235 seats compared with Republicans’ 200.

Democrats face a much narrower path to victory in the Senate, with DDHQ showing a 56 percent probability of winning. Republicans would hold on to 49 seats in this scenario.

articles.title: The silent voter revolt that could upend Congress
articles.summary: a marketplace are coming to the same conclusion. Pollsters have a large number of levers and tools available to them. What they cannot foresee is the discrepancy between what people say and how they will act on Election Day. I
articles.body:
The midterms are fast approaching, and pollsters are sharpening their digital pencils to forecast who will come out on top. Control of both the House and the Senate is in play for both parties. Frequent comments by the president further cloud the situation, as what he says is often not consistent with what people are experiencing. This adds additional uncertainty to an already chaotic process.

Given all this ambiguity, pollsters will almost certainly get it wrong once again, but for a different reason.

Polling is about sampling a small group of people to determine how a large group of people is likely to act. There are four issues that add to its unpredictability, each more challenging to overcome.

First, pollsters ask if a person polled is registered to vote . Next, they ask if the person is likely to vote . Third, they ask which candidates a person is likely to vote for or who they think will win the elections. And the final issue is one over which pollsters have little control: turnout discrepancy and undervoting. This is what a person does when they actually cast their vote and place it in the ballot box, including how they may intentionally choose to not show up or not vote in particular races.

Pollsters have also learned that asking questions directly may not provide the most useful information. That is why they typically ask a series of questions that collectively indicate what a person is likely to do.

Given all such factors, pollsters are constrained to mitigate sampling error by taking larger polling sample sizes , though this cannot correct hidden biases or inaccurate sample targets. The key challenge is matching the sample of people polled with who shows up to vote.

At present, Democrats appear set to win the House and have a growing chance to also take back the Senate . The former is not surprising, given the slim majority held by Republicans in the House , even with all the additional redistricting that occurred in 2025 to mostly protect Republican incumbents. The latter was unthinkable just a few months ago.

Some Republican pundits continue to hold hope for Republicans to hold onto both chambers. Yet with a historically unpopular president asking voters to act like he is on the ballot , hopes for a Republican sweep are fading.

The party of the sitting president typically loses House seats in the midterm elections. Over the past half century, only two sitting presidents have seen their party gain House seats (Bill Clinton in 1998 and George W. Bush in 2002). In 2018, during Trump’s first term, Democrats gained 41 House seats . The resulting Republican headwinds are likely to continue this year.

As much as pollsters are leaning toward Democratic victories, the factors that play into how polls are conducted suggest that the Democrats have an inherent advantage this year that polls may not fully capture.

This is because what people do when they have their ballot in hand may not be something that anyone (including themselves) can ascertain with certainty prior to Election Day. The one group that will determine Democratic gains will not be registered Democrats (they will certainly vote for Democratic candidates) and independents (they may be inclined to vote for more Democrats than Republicans compared to previous elections). The greatest risk for Republican candidates is how unhappy Republican voters — particularly non-MAGA voters like Latinos in states like Texas — will vote or not vote.

A large faction of such voters will continue to support Republican candidates, even though many of them have been personally affected by soaring gasoline prices and their inability to pay their bills (the so-called affordability issue), as well as misguided immigration control by ICE . The group that may stay away are non-MAGA Republicans , who may opt to just not show up to vote, or leave House and Senate races blank. By not voting, they are effectively giving the election to Democrats, making a non-vote a de facto boost for Democratic candidates, particularly in close races.

Midterms typically attract significantly fewer voters than presidential elections . This year will likely be the same, though an unpopular president may provide ample motivation for people to show who up and express their concern at the ballot box.

All these factors point to a clear Democratic victory across the board, even with the structural headwinds of gerrymandering . Prediction markets that report odds based on how people bet in a marketplace are coming to the same conclusion.

Pollsters have a large number of levers and tools available to them. What they cannot foresee is the discrepancy between what people say and how they will act on Election Day. It is such uncertainty that will make their job exceedingly difficult in this year’s midterms, and why uncast ballots may ultimately decide who wields power in Congress in 2027 and 2028.

Sheldon H. Jacobson, Ph.D., is a professor of Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He applies his expertise in data-driven risk-based decision-making to evaluate and inform public policy.

articles.title: Georgia shatters its Day 1 early voting record for a midterm
articles.summary: Georgia set a midterm election record on its first day of early voting Tuesday, with more than 188,000 ballots cast. That is about 50,000 more than the number who voted early on Day 1 in 2022, according to the Georgia secretary of state’s office. Driving the high turnout is Black voters, who made up more…
articles.body:
Georgia set a midterm election record on its first day of early voting Tuesday, with more than 188,000 ballots cast. That is about 50,000 more than the number who voted early on Day 1 in 2022 , according to the Georgia secretary of state’s office.

Driving the high turnout is Black voters, who made up more than 36 percent of Day 1 early votes cast, according to nonpartisan election data site VoteHub. That is more than 6 percent higher than in 2024, VoteHub said.

Georgia is home to some of the 2026 midterm elections’ most closely watched races, including contests for the U.S. Senate and governor.

In the U.S. Senate race, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is fighting to win reelection against GOP challenger Rep. Mike Collins (Ga.) in a state that President Trump won by about 2 points. Republicans had hoped to make the Georgia Senate race competitive given the state’s battleground status, but Ossoff has led in every preelection poll.

Nonpartisan election data site Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, gives Ossoff an 88 percent chance at winning reelection, and he leads by an average of 8.8 points in DDHQ’s polling average.

Ossoff and Collins faced off in their last scheduled debate Tuesday night, hosted by the Atlanta Press Club.

But a much more competitive contest is the Georgia governor’s race. Former Democratic Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms is facing off against healthcare executive Rick Jackson to fill the open seat created by GOP Gov. Brian Kemp’s retirement.

Jackson, who is a billionaire, has far outspent Bottoms in no small part by self-funding his campaign. DDHQ’s forecast gives Bottoms a 57 percent chance of flipping the governor’s mansion, though Jackson leads by 2 points in the polling average.

Georgia home to election integrity questions

The Peach State is no stranger to competitive elections, but it has also been the epicenter of questions of election integrity on both sides.

After the 2020 presidential election, Trump placed a phone call to Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger and asked him to find more than 11,000 votes, the amount needed to overturn former President Biden’s win. Raffensperger refused.

And in the 2018 gubernatorial election, Democratic candidate Stacey Abrams accused Kemp, her Republican opponent, of using his position as secretary of state to suppress voters. A court ruled against Abrams in 2022.

Raffensperger affirmed the strength of Georgia’s election system Wednesday.

“This record-breaking turnout proves that voters have confidence in the integrity of our elections,” Raffensperger said in a statement.

The latest turnout information can be found on the Georgia secretary of state’s election data website .

It’s Wednesday, and put those hoodies and sweaters away if you’re in Washington, D.C., because it is going to be 87 degrees today (it’s Oct. 14….).

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Julia Boehning , filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips to jfeldstein@thehill.com and jboehning@thehill.com .

New data released Wednesday by the Bureau of Labor and Statistics (BLS) showed that inflation rose again in September — with the consumer price index (CPI) increasing by 0.6 percent.

Not only is the CPI up 0.6 percent from last month but is up 3.7 percent relative to September 2025 — well above the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent target.

Energy fuels rise: The Trump administration’s war in Iran has steadily raised regular gas and diesel prices over the conflict’s eight-month timeline. The BLS reported that there was a 9.1 percent increase in gas prices in September, which accounted for more than half of the monthly inflation increase.

Last month, energy prices increased by 5.2 percent as well after rising by 2.1 percent in August.

A gallon of regular gas costs roughly $4.33 as of Wednesday morning, up from $2.98 two days before the Iran war began, according to data from AAA . Diesel costs about $6.30 per gallon, an increase of roughly $2.41 from a year ago.

Madness before midterms: As debate season heats up, Senate candidates are encouraging President Trump to pull out of the Iran war to help lower energy prices.

On Tuesday night, Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) criticized the president’s diesel deal with Russia in her Senate debate against Democratic candidate Josh Turek.

Iowans have been hit hard by the rise in diesel prices, which Trump has attempted to address by making a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin .

“We need to lower gas prices in this country. We need to lower diesel prices, but I don’t think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it,” Hinson said Tuesday night.

Turek agreed, but bashed the GOP candidate for voting with Trump to start the war in the first place. “We are in this situation because of this unnecessary war in Iran that Ashley Hinson voted in favor of continuing seven times,” he said.

Other GOP lawmakers break from Trump: Republican Sens. Mitch McConnell (Ky.), John Cornyn (Texas) and Alan Armstrong (Okla.) were the latest members of the party to oppose Trump’s diesel deal with Russia on Tuesday.

According to The Hill’s Alexander Bolton , the three GOP senators joined a letter to the president, calling the deal a “gift to our adversary and betrayal of our allies.”

Sens. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Lisa Murkowsi ( R-Alaska) and Susan Collins (R-Maine) also signed the letter.

Democrat James Talarico is set to appear in a televised Texas Senate town hall at 8 p.m. EDT, notably without his GOP opponent, state Attorney General Ken Paxton .

Talarico has repeatedly urged Paxton to take the debate stage with him ahead of November’s midterms, even posting a video to social media in which he appeared to call his challenger over the phone before being sent to voicemail.

Throughout Talarico’s flu-induced campaign trail absence last week, even President Trump called for a debate to help settle contentious Lone Star State race — peddling unfounded theories about the Democrat.

Talarico has denied these accusations, saying in a post to social platform X after his absence that he was ready to take Paxton to the debate stage “literally any time, any place, any network.” Tonight’s town hall will be co-hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media.

Debates galore: A day after the president made a rare visit to Alaska to bolster Sen. Dan Sullivan ’s (R) reelection bid, the incumbent will debate his three opponents at 10 p.m. EDT. Sullivan’s locked in a tight race against former Rep. Mary Peltola (D), while their two other challengers — Gerald Heikes (R) and another Dan Sullivan — trail further behind.

Earlier in the evening, gubernatorial candidates in Iowa and Maine will also meet face-to-face. The Democrats in both races are carrying significant leads in their respective races as of this week.

The president is set to make two campaign trail appearances today amid his homestretch campaign blitz.

He will give remarks in Arizona at 4 p.m. EDT before jetting to Montana to speak again at 8:15 p.m. EDT.

Ukrainian officials reported Wednesday that satellites from Elon Musk ‘s SpaceX are slowing down its air defense operations.

The country uses Starshield, a military-grade network of satellite services provided by Starlink.

Speed kills: A source familiar with the situation told The Hill’s Laura Kelly that Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters were impacted, with Starlink services being cut off for objects that traveled faster than 100 miles per hour.

The limitations to Ukraine’s air defense also impacted the country’s ability to defend themselves against explosive drones launched by Russia.

Trump’s threats: On Monday, the Trump administration threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapon sales to Ukraine if they did not stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelensky has defended the strikes as a crucial way of retaliating against Russia.

Trump has told Ukraine to stop the strikes, saying they are causing the U.S.’s diesel prices to rise ahead of November’s midterms. Zelensky has said the Iran war is mostly to blame for global energy disruption.

⛳ A federal judge ruled on Tuesday that the Trump administration must stop work on the East Potomac Park’s golf course, a property the president has looked to redevelop. The administration removed hundreds of trees from the East Potomac Golf Links over the weekend, enraging the judge.

⛽ At his Alaska rally Tuesday night, President Trump pardoned two diesel mechanics previously charged with violating the Clean Air Act. The president signed the pardons for Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming on stage at the event in Wasilla.

❌Advancing American Freedom, a conservative think tank founded by former Vice President Mike Pence, is calling on the Trump administration to reverse their diesel deal with Russia, according to a letter obtained by The Hill’s Helen Huiskes .

✅Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) said during his Tuesday night debate against Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) that he would serve his full Senate term, saying he has “zero interest” in campaigning for the White House in 2028.

💸 The Trump administration announced Wednesday that Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6 percent in 2027.

articles.title: Watchdog files complaint against Zacharia with California bar
articles.summary: The Campaign for Accountability has filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association asking for an investigation into White House press secretary Katie Zacharia over her claims that she is a lawyer after reports surfaced that she is not licensed to practice law in any state. The complaint notes that if the reporting is…
articles.body:
The Campaign for Accountability has filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association asking for an investigation into White House press secretary Katie Zacharia over her claims that she is a lawyer after reports surfaced that she is not licensed to practice law in any state.

The complaint notes that if the reporting is accurate that Zacharia has “repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practice law without a license to do so,” then it’s an act that California law treats as a crime.

“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie,” Campaign for Accountability Executive Director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a statement.

“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime. The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has,” she said.

Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile says she was general counsel of Fix California from 2024-2025, an organization started by Richard Grenell, a former Trump administration official.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

Zacharia’s job history was called into question as she started her job as White House press secretary. The newsletter Popular Information first raised questions about her legal career.

Zacharia held her first press briefing Tuesday, taking questions from three reporters and dropping the news that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to resign. The briefing lasted roughly 14 minutes. Zacharia was criticized by some observers for appearing nervous during the briefing and for calling on just a handful of reporters, some of whom represent conservative outlets.

Zacharia later appeared with President Trump when reporters asked the president how he thought she did and where she passed the bar exam.

Trump deferred to Zacharia, who said it was “when I moved to China.”

A White House official said she moved to China with her husband after graduating due to his job at a U.S. private equity firm, and she worked on international transaction law. Her LinkedIn says she was an associate on the International Practice Team for Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.

Trump also described her as an attorney when he announced she would take over the position from former press secretary Karoline Leavitt.

“Katie is a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University, and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney, and a frequent Commentator on outlets, including Fox News and Newsmax,” he wrote on Truth Social last week.

articles.title: Trump right to share intel with Ukraine; don’t turn off Starlink, Elon Musk!
articles.summary: Devastating Russia strikes hit Kyiv last night, and now 600,000 people are without power. The ballistic missiles were not detected in advance, which meant people on the ground there had little advanced warning. This is very dangerous — I know, because I was in Ukraine several months ago, and I saw firsthand hand how…
articles.body:
Devastating Russia strikes hit Kyiv last night, and now 600,000 people are without power. The ballistic missiles were not detected in advance, which meant people on the ground there had little advanced warning.

This is very dangerous — I know, because I was in Ukraine several months ago, and I saw firsthand hand how the advanced warning of incoming attacks is absolutely critical for the people of Ukraine to go about their lives with even a semblance of normality. Forewarning allows them to seek shelter when appropriate, rather than spending all their time hiding underground.

So it was disturbing to learn that this latest strike was undetected, and there was rampant speculation online that the U.S. had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine , allowing it to prepare for strikes.

President Trump has been very frustrated with the war lately, since Ukrainian strikes on Russia are devastating Russia’s energy infrastructure — this war is destructive for the people of Ukraine and Russia, but also had ramifications for the rest of the world. Nobody likes this, and Trump is right to be upset.

But obviously we cannot pause the sharing of intelligence with Ukraine, which to his credit, Trump realizes. Here was the president confirming that we continue to monitor Russian planes and inform Ukraine of incoming fire.

Trump gets it exactly right there. We must continue to support Ukraine so that we get to a place where Russia will be willing to negotiate to end the war. These terms might not be ideal for Ukraine, but they’ll be better than losing their country. That’s the truth.

There’s another problem for Ukraine, which is that Starlink unexpectedly introduced speed restrictions on frontline combat operations, which will make it more difficult for Ukrainian drones to hit targets in Russia. If this was done intentionally by Elon Musk, it’s a huge mistake.

Remember, it is not Ukraine standing in the way of peace, and here is where we have to be clear-eyed. It’s Russia. Specifically, it’s Vladimir Putin. He could end the war at any time. He could end it tomorrow. If he did that, then Ukraine would stop bombing Russia — we can make them do that. We can’t make them do it if Russia is continuing to invade, but if Russia stands down, then Ukraine stands down. We can have a ceasefire, and bring this horrible conflict to an end.

Again, the choice is up to Putin. And it’s important to remember that, because far too many commentators, including many on the left but also some on the right, act as if Russia has no agency in all this, that they are just reacting to the West or to NATO. It’s not true. It’s Putin’s choice, right now, to cause the deaths of thousands of people, including thousands of Russians.

Then there’s the matter of the Russian diesel deal , with Trump announcing plans to make the diesel available to global markets. The president’s instinct to ease economic tensions for the rest of the world, and indirectly for us, are right. Unfortunately, Russia can invest the profits in the war on Ukraine, prolonging their ability to fight. So from the standpoint of bringing the war to a speedy end, it’s entirely counterproductive to do this, and several Republican and Democratic senators have written a letter to Trump informing him of exactly this.

As much as it pains me to recommend any course of action that raises prices for anyone, anywhere, things are not going to get better in the long term unless they are a little more painful in the short term. We should tell Putin we’d love to buy his diesel, we’d love to make Russia as rich as we possibly can, but we have to hold off on that plan until he gives up his quest to subjugate Ukraine. There won’t be peace until Putin is ready for peace.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Is Russia playing deadly games with the plague? Look to its history.
articles.summary: Following reports of a suspicious death and quarantine at Russia’s Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute, analysts are calling for transparency and international investigation amidst historical context of Russian biological weapons research.
articles.body:
One of the greatest scourges the world has ever known is in recent headlines: the Plague. A technician at Russia’s Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute has died of “pneumonia of unknown etiology ,” nearly 200 people are under medical observation , and the hospital that treated her has been quarantined. Moscow says there is no evidence of the plague and advises everyone to ignore the rumors. The institute handles some of the world’s most dangerous pathogens, including the pneumonic plague, and Russia has a long history of offensive biological weapons research. In a country where asking questions can be hazardous, few answers have been provided.

To understand the questions now surrounding Irkutsk, it is worth remembering that Russia has been asking a darker question for nearly a century: how can disease be turned into a weapon?

Disease killed more Russians than weapons during the conflicts of the early 20th century, and Soviet scientists began exploring its potential as a weapon. By 1928, the Soviet Union was researching, developing, testing, and manufacturing biological weapons, with the plague emerging as a weapon of particular interest, alongside anthrax and smallpox. In 1937, the deputy director of a Soviet military biological institute died after contracting the plague during research; local authorities contained the incident and prevented an outbreak.

During the Cold War, the Soviet Union expanded its offensive biological weapons program. According to Kenneth Alibek , a former deputy director of the program who later defected to the United States, the Soviet Union maintained roughly 20 tons of the plague and sought to make it more deadly through genetic engineering.

Despite signing the Biological Weapons Convention in 1972, Moscow concealed its program behind civilian research institutions, with the KGB monitoring scientists to prevent leaks. The secrecy extended to accidents: In 1979, authorities concealed an anthrax release from a Soviet biological weapons facility that killed civilians.

Russia officially ended the Soviet offensive biological weapon program in 1992, but many facilities associated with it continued operating as research centers. In 2024, satellite imagery showed new construction and renovations at Sergiev Posad-6, a former Soviet biological weapons site where scientists studied smallpox, Ebola and hemorrhagic fevers. Russian officials describe the work as biodefense research, but the facility does not admit international inspectors.

But Russia’s answer to questions about the history of its own biological weapons programs is usually to question what America is up to instead.

In June, Russia’s Ministry of Defense accused the United States of pursuing biological weapons research in Ukraine, including work involving dangerous pathogens such as the plague.

The accusation follows a pattern dating to the end of the Cold War, when Soviet propaganda claimed that AIDS was the result of a Pentagon biological weapons experiment. Decades later, Russian officials revived similar allegations. In 2018, Moscow’s foreign ministry accused the United States and United Kingdom of separate chemical attacks in Syria, a grotesque inversion of the truth. As COVID-19 spread in 2020, Russia accused the United States of using laboratories in former Soviet republics to develop pathogens. In 2022, Russia blamed the United States for the monkeypox outbreak.

Other outrageous accusations include Russia’s claims at the United Nations that the United States considered delivering biological weapons agents through migratory birds and bats. The Kremlin also insinuated that the United States used blood samples from Ukrainians during the Covid pandemic to create weapons that would selectively target Slavs.

In 2022, Russia took those accusations to the United Nations, alleging that the United States was funding a biological weapons program in Ukraine. The United States and its allies rejected the claims as disinformation.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has already asked Russia to share more details on the current situation. President Donald Trump said he is planning to discuss the case with Russian President Vladimir Putin “very soon.” On Tuesday, the U.S. Embassy in Russia instructed Americans in the country to “depart immediately.”

If Washington is taking the situation seriously enough to issue such warnings, it must be pressing Moscow for the information needed to determine what, exactly, is happening. The United States should form an interagency team to monitor the outbreak, analyze health data, and determine its cause and extent. Russia should allow U.S. experts to enter and investigate the outbreak. Given that Russia has already accused the United States of the plague bioweapons program in Ukraine, Washington, and in particular, the Defense Threat Reduction Agency should be prepared to counter Russia’s propaganda.

Russia owes the world a clear account of events at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute. If this was simply a case of pneumonia, Moscow should have little to fear from an independent investigation and transparent reporting. When a death occurs at a laboratory handling potential biological weapons, “trust us” is not exactly a substitute for evidence. And if there really is nothing to see in Irkutsk, Moscow could respond by letting someone see it.

Ivana Stradner is a research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ (FDD ) . Rear Admiral (Ret.) Mark Montgomery serves as senior director of FDD’s Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation (CCTI).

articles.body:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris is set to hit the campaign trail for the last few weeks of the midterms, her office announced Wednesday.

Harris is set to make stops in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin in support of Democrats “up and down the ballot,” her office said.

The announcement comes shortly after former President Obama made several endorsements ahead of Election Day and as President Trump embarks on his own red state campaign blitz.

Harris is set to begin her campaigning stretch in Nevada, planning to appear alongside Democratic gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford on Oct. 21 before traveling to Mississippi the next day for an event with Senate candidate Scott Colom (D). Later in October, she will visit New Hampshire and Wisconsin to campaign with Democratic Senate candidate Chris Pappas and gubernatorial candidate David Crowley (D), respectively

The former vice president will cap the tour “with a series of campaign and voter protection events across the state of Georgia” between Oct. 28-30 alongside Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), who’s seeking reelection this November.

Harris’s campaign blitz comes around two years after she lost the presidential race, an election cycle that left Democrats questioning their future in its wake. However, the party appears to be in a much better position than they were during the 2024 elections.

According to nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ , Democrats are poised to retake both the House and Senate this November. Meanwhile, Republicans are facing political headwinds, including the Trump administration’s unpopular war in Iran and concerns surrounding rising living costs.

The former vice president is also considered one of the top contenders for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, alongside other prominent Democrats, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Ossoff himself, who recently denied such speculation.

articles.title: In Texas, 3 new polls show Talarico with slight lead
articles.summary: New polls show tight contests in Texas in the race for U.S. Senate and governor. Three polls released Tuesday and Wednesday show state Rep. James Talarico (D) leading Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) in the closely watched Texas Senate race. The Texas Politics Project (TPP) at the University of Texas found Talarico leading Paxton…
articles.body:
New polls show tight contests in Texas in the race for U.S. Senate and governor.

Three polls released Tuesday and Wednesday show state Rep. James Talarico (D) leading Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) in the closely watched Texas Senate race.

The Texas Politics Project (TPP) at the University of Texas found Talarico leading Paxton by 3 percentage points among likely voters, 50 percent to 47 percent. That is the same margin TPP had Talarico ahead by among registered voters in August.

A ReconMR/Siena poll found Talarico ahead by 4 points among likely voters, 48 percent to 44 percent, closer than his 6-point lead in the September poll. And a Marist University poll found Talarico leading by 2 points, 47 percent to 45 percent, also closer than his 6-point lead in the Marist’s September poll.

No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994, and the party has not won a Senate race in the Lone Star State since 1988. This year, Talarico’s consistent lead in public polling has the party feeling optimistic about its odds.

The nonpartisan election site Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, gives Talarico a 56 percent chance to flip the Texas Senate seat. He leads by an average of 2.5 points in DDHQ’s polling average.

The Senate race has been considered competitive for much of the 2026 cycle. The Texas governor’s race, on the other hand, was initially viewed as a sure bet for Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

Abbott, who is running for a fourth term in office, has seen his polling lead steadily shrink in recent months as his Democratic opponent, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, continues to gain ground .

The latest polling shows a tight race. TPP’s poll has Hinojosa leading Abbott by 1 point, 49 percent to 48 percent, while ReconMR/Siena has Abbott up by 1 point, 48 percent to 47 percent, and Marist shows Abbott up by 4 points, 49 percent to 45 percent.

Democrats have not won a governor’s race in Texas since 1990.

Early voting begins in Texas on Monday. In 2024, roughly 80 percent of all votes in Texas were cast early. Turnout broke records in this year’s primary voting.

articles.title: Appeals court rules California can’t require ICE to show visible ID
articles.summary: A federal appeals court on Wednesday ruled against a California law requiring Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers to show visible identification, a final ruling after the law was previously put on hold. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit remanded with instructions to enter a preliminary injunction on the state of California, stating…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court on Wednesday ruled against a California law requiring Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers to show visible identification, a final ruling after the law was previously put on hold.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit remanded with instructions to enter a preliminary injunction on the state of California, stating that the federal government has shown that the Golden State’s No Vigilantes Act violates the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution.

The appeals court ruled that the Supremacy Clause “prohibits States from directly regulating federal operations even when regulating state operations in the same manner,” according to the ruling.

“In sum, if a state law directly regulates the governmental conduct of the United States without congressional authorization, it is void irrespective of whether the regulated activities are essential to federal functions or operations, and irrespective of the degree to which the state law interferes with such functions or operations,” the court wrote.

The Hill has reached out to California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s (D) office for comment.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) sued California and Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) last November after he signed the No Vigilantes Act , which demands that plainclothes law enforcement officers operating in California “shall visibly display identification.”

Along with the No Secret Police Act , which banned federal law enforcement officers from wearing masks while carrying out operations in the state, the law took effect on Jan. 1 and required officers to show identification while performing their duties.

The federal appeals court in April sided with the Trump administration in extending its pause on the law until the case was resolved.

Bonta’s office previously told The Hill that good law enforcement requires “transparency and accountability” and accused the Trump administration of stepping “well outside the boundaries of normal practice” with federal law enforcement.

State officials ushered in the law in response to ICE raids throughout the state last year, prompting President Trump to deploy the National Guard in Los Angeles amid protests against ICE operations in June 2025. A federal judge ordered Trump to end the deployment in December.

This ramp-up spilled over to the courts, where the DOJ and California officials have been embroiled in litigation over different aspects of Trump’s crackdown on immigration in the state.

Last month, Newsom signed another law passed in response to ICE being awarded a nearly $17 million contract for 6,000 pairs of electric shock gloves to be worn during immigration operations. The reveal of the gloves in August sparked controversy , with the Democratic governor calling their introduction and use “Orwellian.”

“California is taking action to strengthen transparency, accountability, and oversight around immigration enforcement in our state,” he said in a statement at the time. “This is about stepping up where the federal government has failed our communities.”

articles.title: Nancy Mace’s ex-fiance, 2 other men face sex crime charges after her accusations in House speech
articles.summary: Three men, including Rep. Nancy Mace’s ex-fiance, are now facing charges for a 2018 incident.
articles.body:
CHARLESTON COUNTY, S.C. ( WCBD ) — Three South Carolina men have been charged after Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) accused them in a House floor speech last year of being sexual predators.

John Douglas Osborne, 46; Brendan Patrick Bryant, 53; and Eric Bernard Bowman, 46, have been arrested and charged with sexually related offenses in connection to an incident that occurred on Sullivan’s Island on October 26, 2018, the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED) announced Wednesday.

Affidavits obtained from SLED state that a female victim, 23, had consumed alcoholic beverages, fell into a swimming pool, and eventually passed out on a sofa while intoxicated. She was reportedly unable to speak coherently or walk normally.

While the victim was unconscious, the three men allegedly discussed sexual exploits before agreeing that Osborne would have sex with the victim while the two other men watched, officials said.

Bryant and Bowman allegedly took photographs of the incident, according to arrest affidavits.

Osborne was charged with first-degree assault and battery and two counts of third-degree criminal sexual conduct. Bowman has been charged with voyeurism, obstruction of justice, and publishing the name of a victim of criminal sexual conduct. Bryant was charged with voyeurism.

All three were booked into the Al Cannon Detention Center.

Mace, on the House floor in February 2025, had previously accused Osborne, Bryant, Bowman, and another man of being sexual predators. The fourth man has not been charged, according to Nexstar’s WCBD.

Mace explained that she accidentally uncovered evidence of “rape, nonconsensual photos and videos of women and underage girls” in her South Carolina district allegedly perpetrated by four men.

“When I uncovered evidence of rape and the illegal filming of women, and sex trafficking, I didn’t just see victims. I saw a system that failed to protect them,” she said in her speech. Mace claimed some of the women – including herself – were incapacitated at the time and that she found thousands of images and videos of the alleged assaults taken on hidden cameras.

She went on to say that she was physically assaulted by one of the alleged perpetrators a week later, which prompted her to flee her home and go “into hiding.” Mace had previously shared that she had escaped what she described as a domestic violence situation.

Roughly a month after Mace’s House floor speech, one of the four men she accused sued her for defamation . In April, Mace sued Bowman , accusing him of spreading false information about her after her floor speech.

Then in May, an unidentified woman sued Bryant, Osborne, and Bowman , alleging that they had sexually assaulted her while she was unconscious at Bowman’s Sullivan’s Island home in 2018. The woman, who had been working for Bryant at the time, said she only learned of video of the incident through Mace in 2024.

In August, Bowman turned himself in to authorities to face a felony domestic violence charge in connection with a September 2016 incident. At the time, he was also facing a first-degree harassment charge for an April arrest after he allegedly placed a tracking device on a woman’s car.

Months later, in November, Bryant filed a defamation suit against his ex-fiancée, Mace. In his suit, Bryant claimed that the May lawsuit filed against him, Osborne, and Bowman was fabricated by Mace and Bowman’s estranged wife.
